title: Prospective comparison of Coronary Computed-Tomography-Angiography (CCTA) with Near-Infrared Spectroscopy-Intravascular Ultrasound (NIRS-IVUS) in patients with angina.
summary:
Patients with chest pain are evaluated to determine whether a myocardial perfusion disorder is present. Such symptoms may occur when the coronary arteries—i.e., the vessels supplying the myocardium with oxygen—become narrowed or occluded. The underlying cause is most commonly the accumulation of atherosclerotic deposits (plaques) in the vessel wall or the formation of thrombi. When this occurs, less blood—and therefore less oxygen—reaches the myocardium. If this reduced blood flow persists, a myocardial infarction may develop, during which myocardial tissue becomes ischemic and may die due to insufficient oxygen supply.
To investigate such symptoms, a coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is frequently performed, as is planned in your case. This examination is a CT scan of the coronary arteries, in which the vessels are visualized using iodinated contrast medium and X-ray technology. The method is non-invasive, meaning that no instruments are introduced into the body. In this study, the Philips Spectral CT 7500 scanner (Philips Medical Systems, Netherlands B.V.) will be used.

Prerequisite for participation

Participation requires that a medical indication for an invasive coronary angiography (heart catheter examination, HKU) is already established. This procedure is used to assess the coronary circulation in detail and—if necessary—to perform treatment (e.g., balloon angioplasty or stent implantation) during the same session. As part of this study, a CCTA will be performed before the clinically indicated coronary angiography. This additional CCTA serves to achieve a more detailed assessment of the coronary arteries and is performed exclusively for study purposes. If the CCTA shows that coronary angiography is not required, you will not proceed with the study (you will be withdrawn from participation). 
Coronary angiography is an invasive procedure: a thin catheter is advanced through a blood vessel to the heart, and contrast medium is injected to visualize the coronary arteries. The goal is to determine whether and where a stenosis is present and, if needed, to treat it within the same intervention. As part of routine clinical care, intravascular imaging such as intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) may be used during percutaneous coronary intervention. This guideline-recommended method enables optimal procedural planning and assessment by visualizing the vessel wall and any plaque material from inside the artery.

Use of NIRS-IVUS in the study

Within this study, an advanced intravascular imaging method—near-infrared spectroscopy combined with IVUS (NIRS-IVUS, TVC Imaging System™, Infraredx, Inc., Bedford, MA, USA)—will be performed in all patients. This system represents an extension of conventional IVUS and additionally measures the lipid content of plaques. This is clinically relevant because lipid-rich (“vulnerable”) plaques tend to be unstable and prone to rupture, which may lead to an acute myocardial infarction.
NIRS-IVUS is performed using the same catheter and guidewire as standard IVUS, meaning no additional catheter manipulation or contrast medium is required. The examination is invasive but painless and does not require additional medication. Using the same catheter does not introduce additional risk beyond that of standard IVUS. As with all catheter-based procedures, rare complications may occur, such as vascular injury, bleeding at the puncture site, arrhythmias, vasospasm, or allergic reactions to materials used. Based on current knowledge, no specific additional risks are associated with NIRS-IVUS.
Aim of the study
The aim of this study is to determine how reliably CCTA identifies relevant stenoses and high-risk (vulnerable) plaques, and how accurately it assesses coronary blood flow impairment. For this purpose, CCTA images and quantitative measurements will be compared with the results of invasive coronary angiography combined with NIRS-IVUS. We aim to better understand in which scenarios CCTA performs particularly well and how improved non-invasive diagnostics might help prevent myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular diseases in the future. Ultimately, the study seeks to contribute to safer and more targeted diagnostic pathways for patients presenting with chest pain.
The expected duration of participation for each individual is approximately 24 months.

1. Patient Information and Informed Consent

Before you are enrolled in the study, you will receive comprehensive information regarding all examinations to be performed. You will be informed which procedures are part of routine medical care and which are study-related. Data protection is of utmost importance: all personal and imaging data are pseudonymized, ensuring that they cannot be traced back to your identity.
A key component of the study is the collaboration with the University of Oxford (UK). For this purpose, pseudonymized imaging data will be transferred to research collaborators in Oxford in compliance with all applicable data protection regulations, where a specialized image analysis will be conducted. The CCTA scans of your coronary arteries will be analyzed using state-of-the-art, AI-based image analysis algorithms (CaRi-Research® Software v2.6.2, Caristo Diagnostics Ltd., Oxford, UK). This software is a research-use-only tool and enables highly precise assessment of plaque composition and vulnerability as markers of vascular inflammation. These procedures are explicitly study-related and go beyond standard clinical care and are used solely for research purposes.
Your participation in the study begins only after you have agreed to all aspects of the information provided and have signed the informed consent form.

2. Examination in Chronic Coronary Syndrome (CCS)

If you present with chronic coronary syndrome—that is, chest pain or pressure during physical exertion—you will undergo all guideline-recommended diagnostic procedures, including:
-     Electrocardiogram (ECG)
-     Laboratory testing
-     Transthoracic echocardiography
-     Non-invasive imaging—in this study, a CCTA performed according to clinical indication
These investigations are part of standard clinical care and are not study-related.
Your physician will discuss the CCTA findings with you. If the CCTA evaluation using the Advanced Visualization Workspace – Comprehensive Cardiac Analysis, v15, reveals abnormalities—such as stenosis or suspicious plaque features—coronary angiography will be recommended and performed according to guideline-based standards. As part of the study, this invasive procedure will be supplemented by NIRS-IVUS imaging, which combines intravascular ultrasound with lipid-content analysis of coronary plaque. While IVUS is guideline-recommended for procedural optimization, the detailed lipid quantification is part of the study-specific scientific assessment.

3. Examination in Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS, e.g., NSTEMI)

If you are admitted with an acute coronary syndrome—such as a non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)—all clinically indicated procedures will be performed as usual, including:
-     Electrocardiogram (ECG)
-     Laboratory testing
-     Echocardiography
-     Cardiopulmonary monitoring
-     Coronary angiography
In addition to standard clinical care, this study includes a study-related CCTA performed before the heart catheterization in this patient cohort. This examination is conducted for scientific purposes to allow more detailed assessment of coronary plaque morphology. It is not part of standard diagnostic practice and is performed exclusively within the context of this study.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-	Age > 18 years
-	Stable angina pectoris, CCS class I–III, or
-	Acute coronary syndrome: NSTE-ACS, hemodynamically stable
-	Willingness to participate and ability to understand, read, and sign the informed consent form prior to the planned procedure
-	CCTA performed based on an appropriate clinical indication
-	Indication for invasive coronary evaluation and suitability for coronary angiography and/or percutaneous coronary intervention
Exclusion criteria:
-	Cardiogenic shock and/or hemodynamic instability (Killip class III–IV)
-	Severely impaired renal function: GFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m²
-	Atrial fibrillation at the time of imaging or invasive evaluation
-	Pregnancy, intention to become pregnant during the study period, or breastfeeding
-	Documented intolerance to contrast agents, beta-blockers, or nitroglycerin
-	Significant documented contraindication to intravenous nitroglycerin administration, e.g., severe aortic valve stenosis
-	STEMI within 24 hours prior to the procedure
-	Individuals under judicial or governmental custody in an institution
